analysis.title: The Global Week Ahead (November 20, 2026)
key_insights: Scotiabank argues the Fed's reliance on near-term inflation data could make it more hawkish. Holiday-season seasonal discounting is showing signs of being far less than normal, so seasonally adjusted prices could print hot into year-end.

Tracked US price indexes show discounting this year only in furniture and bedding. Computers, toys, sporting goods, TVs, apparel, cosmetics and appliances show stronger price pressure than in prior years. If seasonal discounting is absent, seasonal adjustment factors could produce very hot CPI readings. Later, the same factors could overcompensate against post-holiday price patterns.

El Niño is probably already adding to US inflation pressure. The author says the Fed may reasonably look through part of the wave as El Niño peaks and wanes by late year. Seasonal adjustment could then overcompensate against a softer later price pattern, which raises the risk that the Committee overreacts.

Canada shows similar signs. Audio equipment, household appliances, and possibly toys and cosmetics are discounted more than in prior years. Electronics, computers and clothing are not, partly because AI investment is raising component demand. This may push Canadian CPI up into year-end, though the evidence is weaker than in the US.

BoC Governor Macklem speaks Tuesday at the Economic Club of Canada, with a press conference. The author expects a carefully hawkish tone that builds on the October decision communications, and says a further hike is likely on December 9th.

The author reads recent BoC communications as hike talk. A staff piece argues there is little cost to front-running a rate response to a supply shock even if the effects prove transitory. Deputy Governor Gravelle said the spillover from commodity prices into core inflation is spreading.

Scotiabank argues Canada's roughly 115k job losses over three months should not hold the BoC back. Its explanations are an outsized and then unwinding youth summer job market, a negative labour supply shock, hiring front-loaded ahead of trade risks, and doubts about the September Statcan figure.

The author argues the labour outlook matters more than the last few months. Defence spending, major projects, data centers and commodity investment could create labour shortages, and Canada may need to raise immigration targets again.

The Bank of Korea is the only central bank deciding this week (Thursday). Consensus expects a 25bp hike after the October pause. Q3 GDP and October core CPI beat expectations, the won is strong against the dollar, and Seoul house prices keep rising. The September Monetary Policy Report signalled appetite for at least one more hike before year-end.

November flash PMIs arrive Monday. The US business activity level is near a five-year high, and the key question is whether it is increasingly accompanied by input cost and selling price pressure. Australia and the Eurozone show softer demand, while the UK and Japan are more resilient.

US releases are crammed into Tuesday and Wednesday before Thanksgiving. They include consumer confidence, October personal income, spending and PCE, Q3 GDP revisions, durable goods, new home sales, the Beige Book and weekly jobless claims.

October PCE and core PCE deflators are both expected up about 0.3% m/m SA. If core PCE is in the right range, it would reinforce FOMC communications leaning toward another hike on December 9th. A lower than expected number could affect rate pricing after an expected December hike.
Eurozone CPI may fall more in m/m terms as gasoline prices drop, but core is expected to stay sticky. Selling price expectations are likely to keep the ECB worried about second-round pressures.

Australian October CPI could approach about 4½% y/y, which could keep the RBA hawkish. The Bank of Japan is primed for another hike on December 18th, and core Tokyo CPI is expected to rise to about 2¾% y/y.
Surging global shipping costs are a common cost-push driver of inflation, with some measures not far off pandemic highs.

US markets are shut Thursday for Thanksgiving, with an early close Friday (1pm ET stocks, 2pm ET bonds). Unofficial early closes on Wednesday would not surprise. Thin participation will be felt across other markets.

tension_points.bull_case: Hot seasonally adjusted readings from reduced holiday discounting and El Niño effects would reinforce hawkish FOMC communications toward another hike on December 9th.
tension_points.bear_case: The Fed may be better off looking through part of the wave. Seasonal factors could then overcompensate against a softer later price pattern, so reacting to the hot readings risks an overreaction.
tension_points.what_invalidates: El Niño peaking and waning by late year and muted holiday discounting effects fading, after which the temporary price pressure should reverse.

tension_points.bull_case: Hawkish BoC communications, staff research favouring front-running supply shocks, and spillover into core inflation point to a hike on December 9th.
tension_points.bear_case: About 115k jobs lost over three months could hold the BoC back from hiking.
tension_points.what_invalidates: The author says Indeed has flagged an unusually early rebound in seasonal hiring that could affect the November jobs print just before the December BoC decision.
